summary: Describes a DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 option and an IPv6 Router Advertisement option that tell a client the address of a captive portal API. Captive portals, as at coffee shops, restrict what users can do until they satisfy some conditions. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join a coffee shop's Wi-Fi, the network usually blocks your access until you open a sign-in page. This document gives the network a way to tell your device that the sign-in page exists, so the device can show it to you without having to guess by trying to reach the Internet.

questions: how do devices discover a captive portal
what is the captive portal dhcp option
what is the captive portal ipv6 ra option
what does the urn:ietf:params:capport:unrestricted uri mean
subtitle: DHCP and router advertisement options that tell a device it is behind a captive portal.

tldr.problem: In a coffee shop or hotel, a device joins a network that quietly blocks most traffic until the user signs in or pays. Today the device can only find out by trying to reach the Internet and being redirected, which is slow, intrusive and increasingly hard to do safely.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines three options that carry the address of the portal's API endpoint: a DHCPv4 option, a DHCPv6 option and an IPv6 Router Advertisement option. The network operator sends them, and the client uses the address to open the portal page directly.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8910 replaces RFC 7710 and moves the DHCPv4 code from 160 to 114, because some Polycom devices already used 160 for something else. The old code is now unassigned.

today: RFC 8910 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 7710 and updates RFC 3679, and it is the current definition of the DHCPv4, DHCPv6 and Router Advertisement options that carry the captive portal API address.

sections.title: Telling the Client a Portal Is There
sections.content:
In many environments offering short-term or temporary Internet access, such as coffee shops, it is common to start new connections in a captive portal mode. This highly restricts what the user can do until the user has satisfied the captive portal conditions, which may involve agreeing to an Acceptable Use Policy or providing billing information.

To present the user with the payment or policy pages, a captive portal enforcement device presently has to intercept the user's connections and redirect the user to a captive portal server, using methods that are very similar to man-in-the-middle attacks. As more attention is paid to security and end nodes adopt a more secure stance, these interception techniques will become less effective or more intrusive.

This document describes a DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 option and an IPv6 Router Advertisement option that inform clients that they are behind a captive portal enforcement device and give the API endpoint that the host can contact for more information. It is not a full solution to all the problems clients have with captive portals; it is one component of a standardized approach, and the methods of satisfying and interacting with the portal are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A captive portal is the sign-in page that a public network puts in front of you before it lets you out to the Internet. Today the network usually intercepts your traffic and redirects you to that page. This document lets the network say where the page is, so nothing has to be intercepted.

sections.title: The Three Option Formats
sections.content:
The Captive-Portal DHCPv4 option has a one-octet code of 114, a one-octet length field giving the length in octets of the URI, and the URI itself, encoded following the rules of RFC 3986. The URI parameter is not null terminated.

The Captive-Portal DHCPv6 option has a two-octet option-code of 103 and a 16-bit unsigned option-len giving the length in octets of the URI, followed by the URI. The URI parameter is not null terminated here either.

The Captive-Portal IPv6 Router Advertisement option has a Type of 37 and a length field that is an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the length of the option, including the Type and Length fields, in units of 8 bytes. The URI MUST be padded with NUL to make the total option length a multiple of 8 bytes, and the URI parameter is not guaranteed to be null terminated.

Because the maximum length of a URI carried in IPv4 DHCP is 255 bytes, URIs longer than that SHOULD NOT be provisioned by any of the IPv6 options described in the document. In IPv6-only environments this restriction can be relaxed.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to send the portal's address, one for each way a device can be configured. All three carry the same thing, a web address, but each packs it into its message format differently, and the router advertisement version has to be padded to a multiple of eight bytes.

sections.title: What the Option Tells the Client
sections.content:
The Captive-Portal option informs the client that it may be behind a captive portal and provides the URI to access an API as defined in RFC 8908. The intent is to improve the user experience by showing the captive portal information faster and more reliably. For the foreseeable future, captive portals will still need interception techniques to serve legacy clients, and clients will need to perform probing to detect captive portals; the mechanism in this document provides a more reliable and performant way to do so and is the preferred mechanism for captive portal detection.

Clients that support the option SHOULD include it in the Parameter Request List in DHCPREQUEST messages, and DHCP servers MAY send the option without any explicit request. Because there are several classes of client, IPv4 only, IPv6 only with DHCPv6 and IPv6 only with RA, the network can provision the URI by several methods, and the operator SHOULD ensure that the URIs provisioned by each method are identical. In all variants of the option, the URI MUST be that of the captive portal API endpoint.

A captive portal MAY do content negotiation and redirect clients that query without an explicit indication of support for the API content type to the value associated with the user-portal-url API key. Such responses might be cached, so the portal SHOULD include an appropriate Vary header field or set Cache-Control to a more restrictive value. The URI SHOULD NOT contain an IP address literal, with exceptions for networks that have only one operational IP address family and where DNS is not available until the portal has been satisfied.

Networks with no captive portals may say so explicitly by using the IANA-assigned URI urn:ietf:params:capport:unrestricted. Clients seeing that value may forego time-consuming forms of captive portal detection.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks for the option while it is getting its network settings, and the server sends back the address of the portal. The device then opens that address itself instead of waiting for a connection to be redirected. A network with no portal at all can send a special reserved address that tells the device to skip the whole check.

sections.title: Precedence of API URIs
sections.content:
A device may learn about Captive Portal API URIs through more than one of the options, or indeed all of them. Implementations can select their own precedence order, for example preferring one of the IPv6 options before the DHCPv4 option or the other way round.

If the URIs learned via more than one option are not all identical, this condition should be logged for the device owner or administrator. It is a network configuration error if the learned URIs are not all identical, which is why the operator is told to make sure that the URIs provisioned by each method are the same.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that gets the portal address by more than one route has to pick one to use, and each implementation may choose its own order of preference. If the addresses do not all match, that is a mistake in the network configuration and it should be reported to the administrator.

sections.title: Registered Codes and the Unrestricted URN
sections.content:
IANA has registered a new entry in the IETF URN sub-namespace for registered protocol parameter identifiers: capport:unrestricted, with this document as the reference. Only one value is defined, and no hierarchy is defined, so no sub-namespace registrations are possible.

In the BOOTP Vendor Extensions and DHCP Options registry, tag 114 is now DHCP Captive-Portal, and tag 160 has been reallocated as Unassigned. The registry note records that 160 was previously assigned by RFC 7710 and is known to also be used by Polycom. The DHCPv6 option 103 and the IPv6 ND option 37, both previously registered in RFC 7710, now reference this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The document assigns the code numbers for the three options and reserves a name for the address that means there is no portal. The DHCPv4 code 160 has been released, because equipment from one manufacturer was already using it for a different purpose.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
By removing or reducing the need for captive portals to perform man-in-the-middle hijacking, this mechanism improves security by making the portal and its actions visible rather than hidden, and it reduces the likelihood that users will disable useful safeguards such as DNSSEC validation or VPNs in order to interact with the portal. Because the system knows it is behind a captive portal, it can also know not to send cookies or credentials. By handing out a URI protected with TLS, the operator can attempt to reassure the user that the portal is not malicious.

Clients processing these options SHOULD validate that the option's contents conform to the validation requirements for URIs, including those described in RFC 3986. Each option is presented using the same protocols used to provision other information critical to a node's configuration, so the security considerations of those mechanisms apply as well. Without measures such as RA-Guard or DHCPv6-Shield, an attacker could inject, modify or block DHCP messages or Router Advertisements.

An attacker able to inject such messages could include an option of this kind to force users to contact an address of the attacker's choosing. Such an attacker could simply list itself as the default gateway, which gives it no significantly more capability, but because this document removes the need for interception the attack may be easier to perform. The operating systems and applications that use this information know that they are connecting to a captive portal device, so they can render the page in a sandboxed environment and clearly label it as untrusted. The means of sandboxing and the user interface are implementation specific and are not covered by the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the portal is announced instead of hidden, the device knows to treat it carefully, and the user is less likely to have to turn off security software to get through. The risk that remains is that someone on the network could inject a false portal address, so the same protections used for the rest of the network configuration apply here too.

viz.caption: The rules that apply to the URI in the option

items.title: Must be the API endpoint
items.text: In every variant of the option, the URI is the captive portal API endpoint.

items.title: At most 255 bytes
items.text: That is the longest URI IPv4 DHCP can carry, so the IPv6 options should not carry longer ones.

items.title: No IP address literal
items.text: The URI should name a host, not an address, except on single-address-family networks.

items.title: Same URI everywhere
items.text: A network that provisions the URI by several methods should use the same value in each.

items.title: Unrestricted marker
items.text: A network with no portal can send urn:ietf:params:capport:unrestricted to say so.
